title: Continuous-time noise mitigation in analogue quantum simulation
source: Nature Communications
abstract: Analogue quantum simulators offer a promising route to explore quantum many-body dynamics beyond classical reach in the near term. However, their vulnerability to noise limits the accuracy of simulations. Here, we establish a continuous-time framework for mitigating noise in analogue quantum simulation. Our protocol fully preserves the continuous-time nature by avoiding any active control or measurement of the system during the dynamics, while achieving exact noise cancellation. This requires a small number of ancillary qubits, whose interaction with the system, combined with classical post-processing of joint measurement data, is tailored to cancel the effect of noise. Furthermore, the protocol is Hamiltonian-independent and robust to realistic ancilla noise. This work points to a promising direction for achieving high-fidelity analogue quantum simulation in the presence of noise.

title: Air-gap engineering enabled ultrafast 9-bit ferroelectric semi-gate transistor array for high-efficiency image denoising
source: National Science Review Advance Access
abstract: The insufficient lateral electric field gradient limits the programming/erasing speed of conventional semi-floating gate transistors, while charge leakage leads to poor data retention and compromised operating characteristics. Here we design a ferroelectric semi-gate (FSG) transistor featuring a triangular air gap adjacent to the drain region. The device exhibits an as-programmed on–off ratio exceeding 107, remaining above 105 after 11 weeks, and a memory window of approximately 6 V. The localized lateral electric field accelerates program and erase operations to 60 ns and 75 ns, respectively. The spontaneous polarization field of the ferroelectric HfZrO layer strengthens charge retention in the HfO2 charge-trapping layer, enabling robust nonvolatile memory performance with a retention time exceeding 106 s. This synergistic integration of air-gap engineering and ferroelectric polarization yields an optimal trade-off between speed, retention and multilevel operation. By exploiting its superior multilevel capability with 9-bit distinguishable current states, we realize Ising-model-based image denoising using a 32 × 32 transistor array. These FSG transistors show promising potential for high-speed, low-power random-access memory applications.

title: Global hotspots and trends of ecological water scarcity in river basins
source: National Science Review Advance Access
abstract: Healthy freshwater ecosystems are crucial for sustainable development, yet they face growing threats from unsustainable water use. However, current water scarcity metrics focus almost exclusively on human demand, overlooking whether sufficient water remains to sustain ecosystems. We address this gap by presenting the first evaluation of ecological water scarcity (EWS) across 1,182 river basins, introducing a novel indicator that recognizes ecosystems as legitimate water users to those of humans. Our findings reveal that in the 2000s, 412 basins (35% globally; 17% annual, 18% seasonal) experienced EWS, with affected areas expanding by 10 million km² since the 1950s. Human intervention intensified EWS in 13% of basins and caused 53% of seasonal and 60% of annual EWS cases. By the 2050s, affected basins range from 392 under RCP2.6–SSP1 to 416 under RCP8.5–SSP5, with persistent hotspots in regions of intensive water use. These findings show that climate mitigation can reduce future EWS risk, but environmental flow protection, water-use efficiency, water recycling, ecologically informed infrastructure operation and ecosystem restoration are also needed to safeguard freshwater ecosystems.

title: Neuronal signatures of successful one-shot memory in mid-level visual cortex
source: Nature Communications
abstract: High-capacity, one-shot visual recognition memory challenges theories of learning and neural coding because it requires rapid, robust, and durable representations. Most studies have focused on the hippocampus and other higher areas. However, behavioral evidence demonstrating links between image properties and memorability and revealing image specificity of visual memory suggests an important role for mid-level visual cortex. We tested the hypothesis that area V4 contains signals critical for recognition memory in two male rhesus macaques. Our task increased difficulty, allowing comparisons of neuronal population responses on correct and error trials. We observed signatures of several proposed memory mechanisms including magnitude coding, repetition suppression, sparse coding, and population response consistency, but only sparse coding and population response consistency predicted behavior. Familiar images also evoked faster dynamics, consistent with pattern completion. These findings demonstrate that fast, high-capacity memory is supported by neural codes in mid-level sensory cortex independent of stimulus features per se, highlighting its role in distributed memory networks.

title: Engineering biocomputability in living and material systems
source: Nature Chemical Engineering
abstract: From subcellular to population levels and beyond, living systems continuously sense and robustly interpret a diverse, ever-changing collection of signaling inputs and produce a near-limitless set of functional outputs. This process, referred to as biocomputation, combines information sensing, transfer and response algorithmically, using modular biological circuitry such as cells, proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules. By hijacking, evolving and repurposing these processes, biologists, chemists and engineers have exploited biocomputational frameworks in a growing number of sectors, including advanced chemical processing, additive manufacturing and tissue engineering. Here we examine the methods by which live cell and engineered biomaterial functions can now be (re)programmed with increased complexity and multiplexability. We categorize approaches based on the type of circuitry used, and highlight the resulting advances in synthetic biology and stimuli-responsive materials. We also explore how these fields have evolved independently but with similar underlying methods and goals, and discuss the exciting opportunities that are emerging from their convergence.

title: Antiviral immunity via telomerase-like reverse transcription in bacteria
source: Nature
abstract: Defense-associated reverse transcriptases (DRTs) employ diverse and distinctive mechanisms of cDNA synthesis to protect bacteria against viral infection1. However, the functions and mechanisms of many DRTs remain unknown2. Here we identify a new antiviral defense system, DRT10, that associates with a noncoding RNA (ncRNA) to catalyze processive, protein-primed synthesis of tandem-repeat DNA. Reverse transcription is templated by a defined ncRNA region with a characteristic sequence pattern and template boundary elements, both of which are conserved and essential for DNA repeat addition. Cryo-EM reconstructions reveal an unanticipated 2:1 architecture, wherein two RT monomers bind opposite sides of a pseudo-symmetric ncRNA. Biochemical experiments further demonstrate that each RT monomer reverse transcribes the template encoded on its respective side of the ncRNA, but only one generates the long repetitive product, whose template is defined by the distance between two flanking stem-loop anchors. This mode of iterative, boundary-delimited cDNA synthesis exhibits direct parallels to the mechanism of telomeric repeat addition by eukaryotic telomerase, and phylogenetic analyses of RTs across domains of life place telomerase in a monophyletic clade with the DRT family, suggesting a common origin for their DNA polymerization activities. Together with earlier studies of DRT2, DRT3, and DRT93–5, our findings identify a conserved mechanistic logic underlying RNA-templated DNA repeat addition across diverse DRTs, despite vastly different architectural solutions, and expand the repertoire of reverse transcription-based strategies for antiviral immunity in bacteria.

title: PDEformer-2: a versatile foundation model for two-dimensional partial differential equations
source: National Science Review Advance Access
abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) are fundamental to modeling physical systems. Traditional PDE solvers are often computationally expensive. Neural operators require independent training for different PDEs, and tend to be data-greedy when adapted to new scenarios. To this end, we introduce PDEformer-2, a versatile foundation model for solving diverse two-dimensional PDEs. The model receives the PDE form as input through a flexible computational graph representation and outputs solutions that can be queried at any spatio-temporal point. Pretrained on a 40 TB dataset spanning varied equation types, domains, boundary conditions, variable counts, and time dependence, PDEformer-2 enables instant zero-shot predictions for familiar PDEs and adapts faster to unseen ones than specialized baselines, achieving lower errors with limited samples. It also facilitates efficient inverse problem solving, successfully recovering unknown PDE parameters, including scalar coefficients and fields, in experiments.

title: Serine-65 phosphorylated ubiquitin associates with soluble tau and seeding activity in Alzheimer’s disease
source: Nature Communications
abstract: Tau propagation is a key driver of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet selective markers of seeding-competent tau remain elusive. Ubiquitin phosphorylated at Serine-65 (pS65-Ub) is a PINK1-derived cellular stress signal that accumulates in AD with elevated tau pathology, but its relationship to tau seeding is unknown. Here, using postmortem brain tissue from female and male donors, we show that a subset of tau is covalently modified by pS65-Ub in AD brain. The pS65-Ub-associated tau population is elevated in AD and is enriched in soluble, high-molecular-weight, oligomeric, and hyperphosphorylated tau species. Across AD cases, soluble pS65-Ub-associated tau levels strongly correlate with tau seeding activity. Tau species isolated with pS65-Ub antibodies exhibit seeding activity, whereas removal of pS65-Ub-associated material markedly reduces seeding from AD brain extracts. Together, these findings identify pS65-Ub as a disease-enriched molecular feature of a seed-competent tau population and link cellular stress signaling with pathological tau propagation in AD.

title: Block-fitness modeling of the global air mobility network
source: Nature Communications
abstract: Accurate representations of origin-destination (OD) passenger flows on the World Air Transportation Network (WAN) are fundamental inputs to models of global mobility, epidemic risk, and infrastructure planning. However, OD data are largely commercial and proprietary, therefore often inaccessible to the research community. Here we introduce a generative model that treats air mobility as a stochastic process within a sparse maximum-entropy framework, informed by aggregate traffic volumes of individual locations and geographic regions. The model accurately reconstructs both network structure and mobility flows, yielding epidemic spreading trajectories that closely match those obtained using real mobility data. Furthermore, the method can be effectively implemented using open data on flight routes and airport traffic, reducing dependence on proprietary datasets. Our approach provides a scalable, interpretable, and computationally efficient framework for scenario analysis and policy design in global mobility systems.

title: The mechanosensitive PIEZO1 channel promotes CD54+/iNOS+ neutrophil expansion in pulmonary fibrosis
source: Nature Communications
abstract: Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) represents the common end-stage outcome of a broad range of interstitial lung diseases. The shared pathophysiologic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identify two phenotypically distinct neutrophil subsets in PF: a pro-inflammatory subset characterized by CD54 (human) or iNOS (mouse) expression, and an alternative subset marked by Arg1 expression. Notably, CD54+ and iNOS+ neutrophils were markedly expanded in PF patients and mice with bleomycin-induced PF, respectively. Adoptive transfer of iNOS+ neutrophils exacerbated fibrosis in bleomycin-induced PF, whereas transfer of Arg1+ neutrophils had no significant effect. Further, the expression of PIEZO1, a mechanically activated ion channel, is predominantly upregulated in CD54+ neutrophils from PF patients or iNOS+ neutrophils from PF mice. Piezo1 ablation in neutrophils selectively impairs iNOS+ neutrophil differentiation, thereby attenuating fibrosis progression. Mechanistically, PIEZO1 promotes the differentiation of these pro-inflammatory subsets through the transcription factor IRF4 in a calcium-dependent manner. We further identify the JAK/STAT pathway as an upstream regulator of PIEZO1 expression in neutrophils. Consequently, PIEZO1 expression and CD54+ neutrophils are markedly decreased in patients treated with JAK inhibitor baricitinib. Importantly, combined inhibition of JAK/STAT and calcium signaling exerts synergistic suppression on the iNOS+ neutrophil expansion and PF progression. Together, our findings reveal a mechanism in which PIEZO1 promotes PF by specifically driving the expansion of CD54+/iNOS+ neutrophils.

title: Flexibility technologies in clean energy systems
source: Nature Reviews Clean Technology
abstract: The clean energy transition has led to increased variability and uncertainty in power systems. In this Review, we describe the technologies and strategies that enable flexibility across clean energy systems and assess global deployment of these technologies, identifying the technical, economic, institutional and social barriers to their adoption. Flexibility is categorized across electricity, natural gas, heat and hydrogen systems, encompassing both supply-side and demand-side resources. Dispatchable generation, large-scale electricity storage and cross-border interconnectors can support flexibility in the power sector; gas networks can deliver balancing services through linepack storage, and electrolysis can convert electricity into hydrogen for storage and later use. District heating integrated with thermal energy storage could potentially serve as a source of flexibility in the heat sector on the hours-to-days timescale. Demand-side response is becoming a scalable and distributed flexibility technology for seconds-to-minutes timescales, enabled by advances in digitalization and decentralization. A whole-system approach is needed to support investment in clean energy flexibility.

title: Cost effectiveness of synthetic fuel and CO2 removal for net-zero aviation
source: Joule
abstract: Aviation's climate impact goes beyond CO2, yet current policies such as the EU's ReFuelEU regulation push almost exclusively toward sustainable fuels, overlooking an alternative: permanently capturing CO2 from the air via DACCS while continuing to burn fossil jet fuel. Comparing long-term costs of both approaches, we find DACCS is 49%–69% cheaper than synthetic fuels and needs far less renewable electricity, suggesting that current policy may be locking aviation into a costlier decarbonization path than necessary.

title: High-frequency inductively heated molten salt bubbling beds for methane pyrolysis
source: Joule
abstract: Methane pyrolysis can produce hydrogen while sequestering solid carbon, but efficient high-grade heat delivery and coking management remain challenging. This study shows that high-frequency magnetic induction directly and volumetrically heats molten salt bubbling beds with stable power delivery, providing a scalable route for methane pyrolysis while managing solid carbon formation. These principles have applicability more broadly to molten salt chemical conversion and thermal energy storage systems.

title: UV/X‐Ray‐Induced Reduction of Eu3+ to Eu2+ in Rare‐Earth‐Based Halide Double Perovskite for Material‐Discriminative X‐Ray Imaging
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Stacked scintillators for x‐ray energy discrimination require at least two emission bands with sufficient spectral separation to avoid signal crosstalk. Rare‐earth‐based double perovskites exhibit narrow‐band luminescence at multiple visible wavelengths, which is advantageous for such designs. However, an efficient narrow‐band blue emission has not yet been realized, hindering further development. Here, efficient Eu
                    2+
                    blue luminescence is achieved in Cs
                    2
                    (Li/Na/K)(Lu/Y/Gd)Cl
                    6
                    under ambient conditions via photo‐induced reduction of Eu
                    3+
                    to Eu
                    2+
                    , eliminating harsh reducing atmospheres. The reduction is driven by 254 nm UV or x‐ray irradiation, while mild heating and x‐ray‐induced lattice distortion assist carrier migration. The unique multi‐cation structure provides cation vacancies that trap holes, stabilizing the reduction. The resulting Eu
                    2+
                    emits narrow‐band blue light at 450 nm (FWHM 25 nm, PLQY 84.1%, 19 000 ph/MeV) in Cs
                    2
                    NaLuCl
                    6
                    , and coexisting Eu
                    3+
                    shows narrow‐band red emission, achieving a 144 nm spectral separation. Taking advantage of this well‐separated dual emission, a stacked scintillator device enables highly material‐discriminative x‐ray imaging.

title: An IscS Persulfide Donates the Sulfur for Ribosomal Protein uL16 Thioamidation
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Posttranslational sulfur incorporation into peptide backbones is increasingly reported. These efforts broaden our understanding of thioamides, which have distinct conformational and hydrogen‐bonding properties compared with amides. YcaO‐catalyzed thioamidation of the ribosomal protein uL16 reportedly occurs across thousands of Pseudomonadota. Here, we identify the cysteine desulfurase IscS, a crucial component of iron–sulfur cluster assembly, as the direct sulfur donor for uL16 thioamidation. Genetic deletion, in vitro reconstitution, kinetic analysis, sulfide scavenging, and mutational studies support this conclusion. Our data support a mechanism in which the IscS persulfide attacks the
                    O
                    ‐phosphorylated uL16 backbone amide to form an IscS–uL16 disulfide intermediate. This labile disulfide is rapidly reduced, and the resulting hemiorthothioamide collapses with phosphate release to give the thioamide. IscS binds uL16 with mid‐nanomolar affinity and can be displaced by other IscS‐dependent sulfur acceptors. IscS promotes formation of the 2:2 YcaO–uL16 complex from the otherwise predominant 1:1 complex. Structural and mutational studies identify uL16 residues important for catalytically competent enzyme–substrate interactions. These findings define the sulfur delivery pathway for uL16 thioamidation and reveal an additional role of the IscS persulfide beyond iron–sulfur cluster assembly, suggesting it serves as another nucleophile for YcaO‐catalyzed backbone modification.

title: Synergistic Regulation of High Dielectric Constant and H‐Aggregation for Efficient and Thickness‐Tolerant Organic Solar Cells
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  While the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of organic solar cells (OSCs) has advanced rapidly, their sensitivity with respect to active layer thickness hinders industrial fabrication. Herein, a novel acceptor BMD‐6F was synthesized via molecular engineering of L8‐BO, which realizes synergistic optimization of dielectric constant (6.20, 1.5 × that of L8‐BO) and H‐aggregation and thus enriches charge transport pathways, facilitates exciton dissociation, and suppresses recombination. As a result, the PM6:L8‐BO:BMD‐6F ternary OSC delivered a champion PCE of 20.34% at 100 nm, and exhibited excellent thickness tolerance with PCEs of 18.23% (300 nm) and 16.18% (500 nm). This work establishes a design principle for high‐efficiency, thickness‐tolerant OSCs, promising industrial applications.

title: Topochemical Engineering of Two‐Dimensional MXenes and Beyond
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Two‐dimensional (2D) materials have gained tremendous attention for their structural diversity and versatile functionality. However, conventional synthesis and post‐synthetic modification often provide limited control over where and how structural or chemical changes occur, restricting the precise tailoring of composition, atomic configuration, and electronic structure. Topochemical engineering offers a distinct approach by directing chemical reactions at predefined sites while preserving key structural features of parent materials, thereby enabling precise and selective modulation at the atomic and molecular levels through four core strategies: conversion, termination, substitution, and transformation. Herein, we present a systematic and critical review of the latest advances in the topochemical engineering of MXenes and other representative 2D materials (TE‐2DMs). We establish the conceptual framework and classification criteria for these strategies and discuss their implementation and underlying structural regulation mechanisms. Special emphasis is placed on the structure–performance correlations of TE‐2DMs in electrochemical energy storage and conversion. We further summarize general design principles and practical guidelines for selecting and implementing appropriate topochemical strategies. Finally, we identify key challenges and emerging opportunities in this rapidly evolving field, with the aim of guiding the rational design of high‐performance 2D functional materials for next‐generation electrochemical energy technologies.

title: Photonic Klein Tunnelling in Silicon Topological Materials for Terahertz 6G Interconnects
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Topological photonics enables robust light transport along engineered interfaces, but transport across a potential barrier placed within such an interface, and the range of barrier strengths over which it survives, remain largely unexplored. Here we experimentally demonstrate photonic Klein tunnelling in a Complementary Metal‐Oxide‐Semiconductor (CMOS) compatible silicon valley photonic crystal at terahertz frequencies. A local, inversion‐symmetric barrier is introduced into a valley kink channel, with its strength Δ controlled through the geometry of the triangular holes. The barrier strength is calibrated using the local Dirac‐frequency shift, establishing a direct relation between photonic crystal geometry and the effective tight‐binding potential. We find that transmission remains close to its barrier‐free value for Δ below the nearest‐neighbour hopping amplitude
                    t
                    , and is strongly suppressed as Δ approaches
                    t
                    . Momentum‐space analysis shows valley pseudospin preserved to better than 98% across two cascaded barriers. We further demonstrate Klein‐tunnelling transport through multibarrier, Ω‐shaped and power‐splitter devices, supporting terahertz data transmission at rates up to 100 Gbit s
                    −
                    1
                    . Our findings underpin a new design framework for resilient and high‐capacity terahertz photonic integrated circuits.

title: Albumin Orchestrates Type‐I ROS Conversion for Efficient Intracellular Bacterial Clearance
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Type‐I photosensitization addresses the dilemma of intracellular bacterial hypoxia‐induced photodynamic therapeutic (PDT) inefficacy, yet precise targeting and eradicating sequestered pathogens remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we engineer an albumin‐based photodynamic conversion nanoparticles integrating target‐specific recognition with controlled antibacterial functions to precisely eliminate intracellular pathogens and restore infected cell activity. Mechanistic studies reveal a vertically‐crossed conformation that promotes intramolecular electron transfer and charge separation, redirecting photosensitizer (PS) reactivity toward type‐I reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Electron‐rich albumin further enhances cationic PS
                    +•
                    recycling, photostability, and O
                    2
                    −•
                    production, while its selective cytoplasmic delivery via receptor/charge interactions enables preferential accumulation in intracellular bacteria, with reduced off‐target organelle engagement. We demonstrate application in
                    S. aureus
                    ‐infected sepsis showing high type‐I ROS levels for antibacterial function from the nanoparticles to restore redox and immune homeostasis without noticeable toxicity. This work pioneers a conformationally‐gated ROS conversion approach for eliminating intracellular bacterial infections, merging mechanistic precision with therapeutic potential for clinical sepsis management.

title: Sustained‐Release Regulation on FAPbI3 Crystallization to Enhance Photo‐Thermal Stability of Perovskite Solar Cells
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Controlling crystallization kinetics of FAPbI
                    3
                    perovskite is crucial for improving crystal quality, device performance and stability. Herein, we report a sustained‐release strategy to regulate the PbI
                    2
                    ‐to‐FAPbI
                    3
                    conversion. PbI
                    2
                    lattice expansion arising from the interaction between PEI (oligomeric poly(ethyleneimine)) and iodide species suppresses nonuniform PbI
                    2
                    crystallization and facilitates FAI infiltration. Moreover, the weak interaction between oligomeric PEGDE (poly(ethylene glycol) diglycidyl ether) and FAI slows the reaction between FAI and PbI
                    2
                    , leading to homogeneous phase conversion during annealing. Consequently, enlarged FAPbI
                    3
                    grains are obtained with improved crystallographic orientation, reduced strain and suppressed nonradiative recombination. Furthermore, released PEI and PEGDE undergo in situ crosslinking to form a three‐dimensional network that passivates grain boundaries, stabilizes microstructure and affords inner encapsulation. The resulting champion n‐i‐p device presents a power conversion efficiency of 26.6% (certified 26.17%). Both films and devices exhibit enhanced photothermal stability. The PEI/PEGDE‐treated device maintains 92% of its initial efficiency at 85 °C for over 1,100 h, 96% after continuous illumination (∼100 mW cm
                    −
                    2
                    ) and maximum‐power‐point (MPP) tracking for over 1,500 h, and 89% after MPP tracking at 85 °C over 12 days. This work offers a polymerization‐assisted route for synchronizing crystallization control, defect passivation and inner encapsulation to enhance perovskite solar‐cell stability.

title: Shedding light on left hippocampal mGlu5 in Alzheimer’s disease
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGlu5) is essential for synaptic plasticity and memory, making it a potential therapeutic target in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). While hemispheric asymmetries in hippocampal function have been observed in AD patients, the lateralized contribution of mGlu5 signaling to cognitive decline remains unclear. Here, we show a physiological left-right asymmetry in hippocampal mGlu5 expression in wild-type mice, with higher levels in the left hemisphere, consistent with previous reports. This physiological asymmetry is lost in two distinct mouse models of AD, the J20 and 5xFAD mice, revealing a hemisphere-specific disruption of hippocampal mGlu5 regulation. Using the light-controllable negative allosteric modulator Alloswitch-1, we show that selective inhibition of left, but not right, hippocampal mGlu5 restores working and short-term memory in AD mice. This finding indicates that altered mGlu5 expression does not simply reflect receptor loss, but rather a dysregulated signaling state that remains functionally relevant and pharmacologically targetable. Left-specific modulation also normalizes pathological downstream signaling, including aberrant Pyk2 and GSK-3β activation and tau hyperphosphorylation, across both hemispheres, indicating a widespread impact of hemisphere-selective intervention. These findings establish a functional lateralization of hippocampal mGlu5 signaling and identify the left hippocampus as a critical site for mGlu5-dependent memory dysfunction in AD. They also highlight the therapeutic potential of region-specific photopharmacology for precise intervention in early AD pathology, providing a strategy for spatially targeted modulation of pathological synaptic signaling in neurodegenerative disease.

title: Field experiments predict ecological response to a large-scale epidemic of an anti-keystone pathogen
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Knowledge of how pathogens, in the context of a changing environment, shape the structure of ecological communities remains limited, and little information exists on the ability of small-scale field experiments to predict the consequences of large-scale environmental impacts. We addressed these issues using the emergence of a widespread epidemic (sea star wasting disease, SSWD) on rocky intertidal shorelines. Prior experiments demonstrated strong reductions in sessile species diversity in response to the local experimental removal of the sea star
                    Pisaster ochraceus
                    [R. T. Paine,
                    Am. Nat.
                    100
                    , 65–75 (1966); R. T. Paine,
                    Oceologia
                    15
                    , 93–120 (1974)] at our site. In surveys of sea star populations over 8 y spanning the onset of the SSWD epidemic,
                    P. ochraceus
                    populations declined by 90%, then subsequently recovered to about one third of pre-epidemic size under an endemic disease phase. Using four different types of temporal data, we documented large increases in populations of the competitively dominant mussel
                    Mytilus californianus
                    following
                    P. ochraceus
                    decline, which were of similar magnitude to those observed in prior field experiments. As in the field experiments, sessile species richness and diversity declined strongly following the onset of the SSWD epidemic as mussels were released from predator control. Our results reveal a strong effect of a pathogen in regulating ecological community structure by disrupting the role of a keystone species, a result anticipated by prior small-scale field experiments.

title: Learning dissipative chaotic dynamics with boundedness guarantees
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Chaotic dynamics, commonly seen in weather systems and fluid turbulence, are characterized by their sensitivity to initial conditions, which makes accurate prediction challenging. Recent approaches have focused on developing data-driven models that attempt to preserve invariant statistics over long horizons since many chaotic systems exhibit dissipative behaviors and ergodicity. Despite the recent progress in such models, they are still often prone to generating unbounded trajectories, leading to invalid statistics evaluation. To address this fundamental challenge, we introduce a modular framework that provides formal guarantees of trajectory boundedness for neural network chaotic dynamics models. Our core contribution is a dissipative projection layer that leverages control-theoretic principles to ensure the learned system is dissipative. Specifically, our framework simultaneously learns a dynamics emulator and an energy-like function, where the latter is used to construct an algebraic dissipative constraint within the projection layer. Furthermore, the learned invariant level set provides an outer estimate for the system’s strange attractor, which is known to be difficult to characterize due to its complex geometry. We demonstrate our model’s ability to produce bounded long-horizon forecasts that preserve invariant statistics for chaotic dynamical systems, including Lorenz 96 and a reduced-order model of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation.

title: Laundering and evasion in response to antislavery policies in Brazil’s cattle sector
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Modern slavery remains pervasive across many economic sectors. Progress toward eradicating it has been partially hindered by a lack of tested, comprehensive policy responses. Using data on millions of cattle transactions in Brazil, we evaluated how ranchers changed their selling behavior after being added to the “Dirty List,” a public registry that names and shames employers found to use modern slavery. Dirty Listed ranchers significantly reduced direct sales to slaughterhouses that signed sustainable supply chain commitments but evaded sanctions by laundering cattle through compliant intermediaries or selling to nonsignatory slaughterhouses. These responses weakened the financial cost of listing to ranchers, and likely allowed beef and leather linked to modern slave labor to enter international supply chains. Our findings highlight the limits of downstream enforcement and underscore the need to monitor upstream suppliers to ensure slavery-free supply chains.

title: AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.

title: Interfacial microenvironments enable abiotic ribonucleoside formation in micro- and nanoscale compartments
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
The abiotic emergence of ribonucleosides remains a central challenge in origin-of-life research because ribonucleosides form inefficiently and are often unstable under prebiotically plausible conditions. Here we show that interfacial microenvironments within aqueous micro- and nanoscale compartments containing D-ribose, phosphoric acid, and nucleobases promote ribonucleoside formation by creating reaction-permissive physicochemical conditions independent of the specific compartment type. Across a diverse range of compartmentalized systems, including gas–oil–water micro/nanobubbles, gas–water micro/nanobubbles, microscale lipid-bilayer vesicles, and oil–water emulsion systems, ribonucleosides form abiotically in the absence of enzymatic catalysis. Under selected interfacial conditions, multiple ribonucleosides, including cytidine, are generated without added catalysts. Comparison among these systems reveals that interfacial architecture and coupled physicochemical properties strongly influence both reaction efficiency and product stability. CO
                    2
                    -based micro/nanobubbles support sustained cytidine accumulation, highlighting the importance of coupled gas–liquid and liquid–liquid interfaces. Ribonucleoside synthesis also depends on compartment size, whereas variations in oil content within micro/nanobubbles selectively modulate inosine formation, underscoring the sensitivity of nucleoside chemistry to interfacial properties. These findings identify interfacial microenvironments within micro- and nanoscale compartments as a general physical framework for ribonucleoside emergence and suggest that ubiquitous compartmentalized interfaces on early Earth could have provided robust settings for prebiotic ribonucleoside chemistry.

title: Multidimensional vulnerabilities of informal settlements in the Urban South
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Informal settlements are widespread and rapidly growing, often associated with high vulnerabilities. However, global-scale understanding on their spatial distribution and complexity of vulnerability is limited. Here, we delineate the informal settlements across a sample of 1,914 cities of the Global South by integrating Sentinel-2 imagery with deep learning models, and we explore the heterogeneity of vulnerability using Urban Informal Settlement Vulnerability Index that encompasses living conditions, social infrastructure, and environmental risk. We found that Urban Informal Settlements cover 12.94 ± 2.52% of their total urban areas (approximately 34.04 × 10
                    3
                    km
                    2
                    ), especially in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Middle Asia. Sub-Saharan African cities have the highest vulnerability of informal settlements, with 31.75 ± 6.20% of total urban areas being occupied by informal settlements, while East Asian cities exhibit relatively low vulnerability across all dimensions. We also find that urban informal settlements with high environmental exposure are widespread in the Global South, and there is a significantly polarized distribution between “low” and “high” vulnerability categories. The findings highlight the disparate distribution of multidimensional vulnerability in informal settlements across the Urban South, providing a comparative evidence base for further local assessment and context-specific policy discussions related to SDG 11.

title: In mice, a population of male germ cells show characteristics of nonapoptotic cell death during G0 arrest
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: In mammals, a small population of spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) is established shortly after birth. These cells self-renew and produce sperm for the male’s reproductive lifespan, passing the genome on to the next generation. Establishment of a population of SSCs with high genomic integrity is essential. SSCs are derived from a much larger precursor population of male germ cells (MGCs) that differentiate during fetal life. During the last third of gestation, MGCs undergo a prolonged period of G0 cell cycle arrest during which they sustain high levels of transcription and acquire epigenetic programming for SSC fate. Although these differentiation steps can cause cellular and genomic damage, it has been unclear whether selection for germ cell quality occurs during G0 arrest since no classic markers of cell death have been detected. In this study, we used a mouse model to characterize a population of MGCs that begin to accumulate markers of cell death, such as AnnexinV (AnV) and propidium iodide (PI), at E16.5. The AnV- and PI-positive MGC population is characterized by low expression of the RNA-binding protein, Dead End 1, and exhibits dsDNA breaks and mitochondrial dysfunction. Interestingly, we do not see evidence of an active cell death cascade until the time of birth, when phosphorylation of MLKL, a hallmark of necroptotic cell death, occurs. Based on these findings, we propose that variable cellular health is an important basis for selection of SSC precursors.

title: Evolution shapes ecosystem resilience through spatial self-organization
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Drylands are globally widespread and ecologically important but vulnerable to climate change. Many exhibit spatially self-organized vegetation patterns that enhance resilience by enabling vegetation to reorganize their patterns under drying, thereby optimizing water use and maintaining productivity. Plants can also undergo evolution in response to environmental change. Although both spatial self-organization and rapid evolution are fundamental mechanisms of resilience, their interaction remains largely unknown. Using a theoretical model, we examine how these mechanisms interact to shape vegetation transitions—abrupt or gradual—and ecosystem resilience under climatic drying. We find that pattern formation can suppress adaptation by maintaining soil moisture beneath vegetation patches despite rainfall decline, thereby limiting selection for increased drought tolerance. However, this suppression is largely alleviated under the variable rainfall typical of drylands. In turn, evolution feeds back on self-organization by increasing the spatial plasticity of vegetation patterns and their ability to reorganize under changing climate, although this positive effect weakens as evolutionary rate increases. Considering direct (adaptation) and indirect (pattern-mediated) effects, evolution enhances resilience, with indirect effects via pattern plasticity dominating. Within model scenarios spanning plausible rainfall variability and relative evolutionary-to-ecological rates, more than half of vegetation transitions are abrupt involving biomass losses exceeding 50%, highlighting a potential mechanism underlying recent global observations of widespread abrupt vegetation losses in drylands. These results demonstrate that evolution and spatial self-organization jointly determine dryland resilience under environmental change and highlight the unexpected role of evolution in patterned landscapes, calling for integrative approaches to predict ecosystem responses in a changing world.

title: Cell identity competes with surface tension to determine stromal organization in tumor spheroids beyond the CAF shell paradigm
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are often found forming a peripheral stromal barrier around tumors. Here, this paradigm is challenged using microfabricated 3D cancer–CAF spheroid models combined with quantitative magnetic force tensiometry. A surface tension atlas is established for eight cancer cell lines, three CAF populations, and heterotypic tumor–CAF assemblies, spanning nearly two orders of magnitude. Surface tension is first shown to govern spheroid morphology and modulate drug response. Besides, CAFs consistently occupy the highest end of the surface tension hierarchy, predicting core rather than peripheral localization and directly challenging the shell paradigm. Yet confocal imaging reveals not only central accumulation but also complete CAF-tumor mixing, including in spheroids where cancer cells exhibit surface tensions nearly two orders of magnitude lower than CAFs. Surface tension alone therefore fails to predict CAF organization. Instead, the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) state of cancer cells emerges as a major determinant: epithelial-like tumors promote CAF core accumulation, whereas mesenchymal-like states favor persistent mixing. Peripheral CAF localization emerges only under restricted conditions combining high tumor cohesion and sequential stromal recruitment. Together, these results identify surface tension, EMT state, and assembly chronology as joint determinants of tumor–stroma architecture, revealing a context-dependent organization landscape rather than a universal CAF shell.

title: The honey bee stinger: An unusual pump with collapsible double pistons
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Most stinging animals deliver venom by contracting muscles around a venom reservoir, but honey bees employ a fundamentally different strategy. The stingers of worker bees have the unique ability to autotomize, separating from the body, to continue to sting independently. Despite more than a century of anatomical descriptions, the mechanics of venom pumping have remained unresolved due to the challenges of observing them in action. We recorded high-speed videos of active, autotomized stingers, combined with micro computed tomography-based three-dimensional reconstruction to characterize the biomechanics of stinging in the honey bee
                    Apis mellifera
                    . We reveal that the stinger functions as a unique double-piston micro-pump. Two lancets, each possessing a deformable valve, slide in antiphase within a bulb chamber. These valves dynamically deform to alternately form a seal during the downstroke and collapse during the upstroke, enabling pressure generation for pumping while potentially minimizing backflow during refilling. The inverted tear-drop shape of the bulb facilitates refill even while pumping proceeds. We explored valve deformations and flow behavior by constructing a dynamically scaled physical model of the bulb chamber confirming key features of the pumping cycle and propose mechanisms for valve deformations. The double piston design adds significant design complexity but enables continuous venom delivery in a compact, autonomous unit. These findings provide deeper understanding of venom pumping in honey bees and other Hymenoptera. This study also provides evidence of an axial piston pump within a biological system and offers inspiration for the design of microfluidic pumping devices.

title: Nonclassical growth to mesoporous quasi-single crystal CeO2 superstructures with a well-defined surface
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Single-crystal materials are essential for fundamental catalysis studies and advanced technologies; however, synthesizing single crystals that simultaneously integrate mesoporosity, tunable size, and well-defined surfaces remains challenging. Here, we report a wet-chemical, template-free strategy to synthesize mesoporous quasi-single-crystal CeO
                    2
                    superparticles (SPs). Operando wide- and small-angle X-ray scattering combined with theoretical modeling reveal a nonclassical growth mechanism driven by the oriented attachment of nanocluster building blocks. This process yields high-surface-area quasi-single crystals that preferentially expose energetically favorable (111) facets on both the external surfaces and internal pore walls, thereby enhancing the stabilization of active sites when used as heterogeneous catalyst supports. Using this approach, we demonstrate broad applicability by synthesizing highly dispersed precious metal–loaded CeO
                    2
                    (M/CeO
                    2

                    2

                    2
                    hydrogenation to methanol, delivering a high methanol selectivity of 85% and markedly improved durability compared with conventional supports.

title: Integrating cooperative breeding with reciprocity and culture extends Hamilton’s rule to humans
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: We study how kinship and reciprocity shape giving and child care support in societies with limited access to markets. Extending Hamilton’s rule to incorporate reciprocity, we test it using behavioral data from dictator games and surveys in remote matrilocal and patrilocal villages of northeast India (N = 406 parents of young children). We replicate with data from urban Manila neighborhoods (N = 301) and the Solomon Islands (N = 624). Consistent with predictions, transfers to recipients increase with genetic relatedness to the donor and even more with relatedness to the donor’s child—a hallmark of reciprocity anchored in shared genetic investment. Nonanonymous conditions amplify giving, especially to nonkin. Cultural norms shape cooperation, but do not trump genetic relatedness. These results underscore the role of affinal ties and reciprocal exchange in sustaining cooperation, and suggest a mechanism through which cooperative breeding could contribute to the emergence of generalized reciprocity and human sociality.

title: Structural insights into the coupling mechanism of vectorial CO2 uptake by DAB1
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
